question: In its special report on the rule of law in the EU1, the European Court of Auditors indicated that the Commission had carried out an initial screening for ‘breaches of the principles of the rule of law’ for all 27 Member States. It then conducted more in-depth analysis and carried out additional investigations for four Member States.

In 2023, the Commission had taken official actions under Article 6(4) of the Conditionality Regulation for Hungary and Poland and launched a procedure for Hungary. The report explains that ‘in principle, this “staged” approach is in line with the Conditionality Regulation. However, we consider that the Commission should specify its criteria for advancing from one stage to the next. This has not been the case so far.
Can the Commission confirm that the way it judges Member States when they ‘contravene’ one of the European values is completely subjective?
On what criteria does the Commission base its sanctions of countries that ‘breach the rule of law’ and what is the legal basis for these criteria?
Can the Commission confirm that it exercises its capacity to block funds only against countries whose governments are not in the political majority governing the EU institutions?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2024) 1. Since 1 January 2021, under the Conditionality Regulation1, the Commission is responsible for proposing to the Council the adoption of measures to protect the EU budget in case of breaches of the principles of the rule of law in Member States. The Commission assesses the situation strictly in line with the conditions set by the co-legislators.

The Regulation applies where breaches of the principles of the rule of law affect or seriously risk affecting the sound financial management of the EU budget or the protection of the financial interests of the EU in a sufficiently direct way.

Furthermore, the Commission can initiate a procedure under the Conditionality Regulation only if other instruments existing under EU law cannot protect the EU budget more effectively. 2. The Commission does not and cannot impose sanctions under the Conditionality Regulation.

It can only propose to the Council to adopt appropriate and proportionate measures to protect the EU budget in case breaches of the principles of the rule of law in a Member State affect or seriously risk affecting the EU financial interests, as defined by the Conditionality Regulation. The Council then takes the final decision on the measures.

The Commission has also published guidelines2 to explain how it interprets the Conditionality Regulation. 3. The Conditionality Regulation establishes which breaches of the principle of the rule of law and their link with the EU budget are relevant for the Commission’s assessment.

For instance, relevant breaches include failing to prevent, correct or sanction arbitrary or unlawful decisions by public authorities, or failing to ensure the absence of conflicts of interest, or limiting the effective investigation, prosecution or sanctioning of breaches of law.

These breaches must concern specific situations, for instance the proper functioning of the authorities carrying out financial control, monitoring and audit or the proper functioning of investigation and public prosecution services in relation to the investigation and prosecution of fraud, corruption or other breaches of EU law relating to the implementation of the EU budget.

The Commission must assess these criteria in an objective, impartial and fair manner, as also stated in the special report of the Court of Auditors cited by the Honourable Member. The Commission applies the Conditionality Regulation in accordance with the criteria set therein by the co-legislators. This is line with the very principles of the rule of law.
The Commission does not make a scrutiny of a political nature of any Member State.
